content_voiceover: This slide covers RBC inclusion bodies — high-yield because boards love asking what an inclusion is made of and what stain reveals it. Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants, a single round basophilic dot, classically seen after splenectomy or with hyposplenism, as well as megaloblastic anemia and hemolysis — the spleen normally pits these out, so their presence signals impaired splenic function. Basophilic stippling is residual RNA and ribosomes, seen in lead intoxication, thalassemia, and other abnormal heme synthesis states like sickle cell disease or MDS. Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing siderotic granules, visible on Prussian blue stain, seen after splenectomy, in hemolysis, sideroblastic anemia, and MDS. HbH bodies are beta-globin tetramers, beta-4, visible only with supravital stain, giving a golf-ball appearance, and are diagnostic of HbH disease in alpha thalassemia. Heinz bodies are precipitated denatured hemoglobin, supravital stain only, classically from G6PD deficiency under oxidant stress, unstable hemoglobin in alpha thalassemia, and chronic liver disease. Fessas bodies are alpha-globin tetramers, alpha-4, supravital only, specific for beta-thalassemia major. Crystals indicate hemoglobin C disease. Cabot rings are mitotic spindle remnants, seen in MDS and megaloblastic anemia. The key distinction to memorize: DNA is Howell-Jolly, RNA is basophilic stippling, and iron is Pappenheimer — same post-splenectomy setting but three different stains and contents.
keypoints: Basophilic stippling = RNA → lead poisoning, thalassemia
Pappenheimer body = Iron (Prussian blue) → splenectomy, sideroblastic anemia
HbH body (β4) vs Fessas body (α4) — supravital stain only
Heinz body = denatured Hb → G6PD deficiency, oxidant stress
keypoint_voiceover: Key points on RBC inclusion bodies. Howell-Jolly bodies are DNA remnants seen after splenectomy or hyposplenism. Basophilic stippling is RNA, classic for lead poisoning and thalassemia. Pappenheimer bodies are iron granules on Prussian blue stain, also linked to splenectomy and sideroblastic anemia. HbH bodies are beta-four tetramers marking HbH disease, while Fessas bodies are alpha-four tetramers marking beta-thalassemia major, both visible only with supravital stain. Heinz bodies are denatured hemoglobin, the hallmark of G6PD deficiency under oxidant stress.
